claims.text: Greater surface compositional heterogeneity or segregation causes high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles to begin premelting at lower temperatures than nanoparticles with homogeneous surfaces.
High-entropy alloys contain five or more principal metallic elements.
Rapid quenching produces a near-homogeneous elemental distribution in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Slow annealing in an inert or vacuum environment promotes controlled surface segregation while leaving the nanoparticle core composition largely unchanged.
Thermal processing induces elemental segregation at the nanoparticle surface.
Surface-segregated regions have lower cohesive energy and weaker atomic bonding than compositionally uniform surface regions.
The localized reduction in surface bonding strength lowers the energy barrier for atomic diffusion.
A lower barrier for surface atomic diffusion advances the onset of premelting.
Slow-annealed, surface-segregated nanoparticles will have a lower premelting onset temperature than rapid-quenched, homogeneous nanoparticles.
The difference in premelting onset can be detected using in situ microscopy or calorimetry.
Rapid-quenched nanoparticles have a near-uniform surface composition and a relatively higher premelting onset temperature.
The proposed relationship should hold for high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles with sizes on the order of tens of nanometers.
The proposed relationship should hold for compositions containing more than five principal elements.
The relationship applies from the onset of surface atomic rearrangement through complete melting under inert or vacuum conditions.
Atomic-size mismatch and element-specific interactions may influence the magnitude of the segregation-induced temperature shift.
Nanoparticle-support interactions may affect observed thermal behavior.
High-entropy-alloy nanoparticles are relevant to catalysis, chemical sensing, and energy-conversion applications.
DSC endothermic peaks can identify the onset temperature of nanoparticle premelting.
TEM with EDX mapping can track surface rearrangements and quantify surface segregation during heating.
Failure of the surface-segregated nanoparticles to show a lower premelting onset or altered surface-premelting behavior relative to the homogeneous control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The initial material class includes nanoparticles with five or more principal elements, whereas the stated boundary restricts applicability to more than five, inconsistently treating exactly five-element alloys.
